summary:
**Conversation Overview**

This was a wide-ranging technical and creative conversation covering two main threads: a deep design discussion about No Man's Sky's procedural generation architecture and a practical session on optimizing the player's current ship builds. The player is a highly experienced NMS player on Xbox who self-describes as extraordinarily wealthy in-game (approaching a billion credits, having just crossed 53 million), with a strong preference for hands-on experimentation and direct, no-nonsense communication. They pushed back on Claude multiple times when responses were inaccurate or hedged, and Claude corrected course several times based on their firsthand gameplay knowledge.

The design discussion began with the player challenging Claude's assertion that NMS planets don't evolve, ultimately leading to a productive collaborative analysis. The player correctly identified that NMS's generative codebase has a genuine evolutionary lineage across patches rather than being purely static, and proposed a compelling system: building an Atlas AI trained on NMS's entire update history (analogous to how large language models are trained on human history) to serve as a fitness function judge for procedural generation, eliminating the need for manual content updates. The player further refined this with a community feedback mechanism — a single rate button in the ship catalog next to the existing upload/name options — to provide continuous live preference signal. They also proposed launching this as a community expedition called "Birth of Atlas" running up to six months to maximize player engagement. Claude acknowledged this as the most coherent version of the "replace the patch cycle" proposal discussed, with the honest remaining gaps being reward-hacking defense and the inability of a judge to originate genuinely new mechanic categories.

The practical gameplay session covered the player's current ship fleet and build optimization. They own a canary yellow S-class Sentinel Interceptor obtained during a recent expedition, plus a second interceptor that mysteriously vanished and reappeared on their freighter reskinned black and smaller after about a week. They successfully duplicated a Flawless Antimatter Injector and a 318 Flawless Pressure Inverter by transferring the expedition interceptor into their main save and stripping its tech. Their current Positron Ejector build is achieving 10,194 DPS with two touching supercharged slots plus a third adjacent upgrade, none of which are flawless-tier modules, leaving room for further improvement. Their hyperdrive build uses the Emergency Warp Unit and colored drives (Cadmium, Emeril, Indium, Crimson Core) arranged around two supercharged slots with S-class 320 LY range upgrade modules in those slots, with a third upgrade placed adjacent to the Indium Drive after discovering the optimal slot wasn't truly adjacent. The player also mentioned losing a beloved canary yellow needle-class S-class ship with 2,200 LY range and 460 damage potential to what appears to be a glitch, with base screenshots as proof of its existence. Their preferred combat style is boost-brake-180-reboost with the inertial dampener toggle (called the "drift module" or similar) to go backward at speed, closing to point-blank range for Positron Ejector use, which they noted requires care around freighters due to friendly-fire clipping. They are seeking PvP ship combat against community players but have been unable to get anyone to accept challenges.

Several corrections to Claude's responses occurred: the player corrected that you cannot dig for Salvageable Scrap from inside your ship (you must get out on foot); that Sentinel Interceptors cannot be obtained or outfitted at stations but must be found as crash sites on dissonant planets; that the in-game "Damage Potential" stat and forum-calculated DPS figures are completely different measurements on different scales; and that the exact placement of base drives relative to upgrade modules does affect which drive receives adjacency bonuses, making the Indium/Emeril/Emergency Warp Unit positioning a real stat decision rather than cosmetic. Claude also initially overstated the Emergency Warp Unit's superiority without acknowledging uncertainty about the Crimson Core's specific link percentage, which remains unconfirmed. The player prefers direct acknowledgment of corrections without hedging, and responds negatively to responses that feel defensive or dismissive of their firsthand observations.

The game also boasts complete solar systems, varied weather systems, detailed flora and fauna, fascinating alien creatures, as well as fully functioning buildings and spacecraft. Indeed, No Man’s Sky plots the position of stars and their stellar classification, while pseudorandom numbers generated from the position of each star are used to determine the planetary system and corresponding features. “The universe begins with a single input, an arbitrary numerical seed—the phone number of one of the programmers. That number is mathematically mutated into more seeds by a cascading series of algorithms—a computerized pseudo-randomness generator,” Roc Morin of The Atlantic explained in a detailed article about the game.

No Man's Sky features a procedurally generated open universe of 18 quintillion planets, which means the game is generated algorithmically rather than manually. It is the first game to use procedural generation to the extent it does.[1] Nearly all elements of the game are procedurally generated, including solar systems, planets and their ecosystems, flora, fauna and their behavioral patterns, artificial structures, and alien factions and their spacecraft. The game's engine employs several algorithms that can mimic a wide range of geometry and structure found in nature. Art elements created by human artists are used and altered as well within these generation systems. The game's audio, including ambient sounds and its underlying soundtrack, also use procedural generation methods from base samples developed by Paul Weir and the musical group 65daysofstatic.

Whilst procedural generation will start from scratch for any new visitor to a planet, the initial factors being fed into the algorithm should be identical, such that each character will see the same types of creatures and behaviours, if not the identical individuals (unless two characters are close enough to each other); indeed it appears that species extinctions are not possible. The game’s art director, Grant Duncan, told Gameinformer:[3] ”When it came to creatures, we built the kind of creatures that exist on the Earth... and it's quite surprising how few different types of skeletons there are.” Gameinformer further notes, “Hello Games looked at these basic templates (i.e. skeletons) – which they call blueprints – as the basic foundational essence of their creatures.” TheSeaOfThySoul goes on to add that these blueprints, can be fed into this system, interacting with each rule before they end up as an animal or plant in an environment that suits them...

As height changes, weight can change, the proportions the animal has can change, as this changes the animations can change, the bones can get bigger, thicker, and the voice can get deeper, etc. What is the environment like? What kind of creature is it? Where is it in the food chain? What will it prey on, what will prey on it? How will it interact with other creatures? As this blob is fed through the system you’re creating an animal that will make sense in the end, which even has behaviours, a male and female of the species, and variation among the species, for instance one might be a bit taller, have longer horns, etc. Animal L to R: Template - Accessories - Layering - Scaling · At the detailed level, Grant Duncan[4] has talked about two levels of procedural generation - one which creates terrain, and another which adds props (i.e. everything else).

content.title: The Wonders of Worlds: Creation and Procedural Generation in No Man's Sky
content.text:
From this seed, each star system, planet, creature, or space station (among other elements of the game) are generated upon a player's first visitation. This means that if you are the first player to ever visit a star system, you have effectively ...

The initial release of No Man’s Sky was disastrous in nearly every conceivable way (review bombings, an investigation, and even death threats). But in a story of resilience for the ages, the team’s post-launch development has been nothing short of a redemption arc, because rather than taking the money and running for the hills (like so many development studios before), Hello Games dug in their heels amidst immense backlash and spent years grinding away at free updates for the community. These free updates have included complete overhauls to combat, the introduction of new game modes and gameplay mechanics to keep the game fresh, and major advancements in graphics and performance (among plenty others). On a personal level, I found their Companions update quite charming, in so far as it introduced alien pet companions to the game. Now, all these kooky and cute creatures I was stumbling upon planet-hopping, had a purpose behind merely surveying and cataloguing.

From this seed, each star system, planet, creature, or space station (among other elements of the game) are generated upon a player's first visitation. This means that if you are the first player to ever visit a star system, you have effectively prompted the conditions for that star system's very creation. The characteristics of that creation, whether it is the deep crevices along planetary seafloors, the roaming herds of aliens, or the hues of grasses being flicked around by the wind, are generated using a series of algorithms produced by HelloGames themselves. These algorithms are altered from time to time to change the possible combinations allowable within the game engine. Back during their Origins update, their adjustments to procedural generation refreshed the entire universe, including previously visited and colonized planets, resulting in chaos as pristine sand-swept beaches could be utterly transformed into hostile volcanic hellscapes.

This is not to say that HelloGames is not designing creature models, multi-tools, weather effects, the textures of water, the sky's palette, or the visual components of a starship - far from it. But their procedural-generative engine is at the heart of their design and remixes possible combinations to create unique variance when the player engages with the world. With the recent Worlds Part 1 & 2 updates, HelloGames have again, but more dramatically, altered the procedural generation engine to not only vastly expand the size and scope of their worlds, but transformed them through greater diversity than anything previously seen. This diversity is needed, because as varied as this engine might initially appear, players spot continuity in design and notice similarities over time. For example, whilst a model for a cacti can be exceptionally varied on an arid planet, the unique characteristics of that cacti would be rendered unidentifiable with repeated visits to different arid planets.

It's a fair question. Let's review the fundamentals of No Man's Sky's world design. At the heart of the game's galactic vastness, which allegedly contains 18 quintillion planets (though counting would be a fool's errand), is their procedural generation engine. For those out of the loop, procedural generation is "a method of creating data algorithmically as opposed to manually, typically through a combination of human-generated content and algorithms coupled with computer-generated randomness and processing power." Most video games have manually created worlds developed for players to inhabit or play through. This could include the village of Stardew Valley, a crowded player hub in Guild Wars 2, or a multiplayer map for Battlefield 1. In fact, this is often so apparent that it is considered the default understanding of video game development for many people.

Most of the universe in No Man's Sky is procedurally generated, including solar systems, planets, weather systems, flora (plants) and fauna (animals) on these planets, the behaviour of these creatures, and artificial structures like buildings and spacecraft. The generation system is based primarily on providing a single seed number to their deterministic engine which would create all the features of the universe exactly the same way every time this process is run with the same seed using the repeatability of pseudorandom number generators. One generator is used to create the universe, plotting the position of the stars and their stellar classification, using the phone number of one of the Hello Games' developers as the founding seed. Pseudorandom numbers generated from the position of each star are used to define the planetary system the star has, the planet's position is used as a seed to define the planetary features, and so on.

The planet terrain generation code, for example, is only 1,400 lines of code; as described by Murray, the code was tweaked as to make sure that planets generated visually interesting but navigable terrain, as some early builds would produce wildly stunning planets that were impossible to traverse, while other fixes made planets look flat and dull. Hello Games had originally planned to use a 32-bit seed number, which would have generated around 4.3 billion planets, but decided to use 64-bit number to demonstrate the scalability of their game, and partially in response to online forum comments that doubted that Hello Games could deliver a game of that size. The deterministic approach also allows Hello Games to optimize the rendering of the game, as what is visible to the player can be determined directly through these generation algorithms. Planets are rendered using voxels with procedurally-generated textures while flora, fauna, and other surface features use polygon-based rendering as 

The generation system uses deterministic parameterised equations and algorithms previously developed by biologists and physicists that can mimic a vast array of natural forms and shapes. For example, the engine uses L-systems, fractal equations developed by Aristid Lindenmayer in 1968 that can create structures that resemble many algae and plant lifeforms. This is coupled with engines like SpeedTree to create additional variety to the flora. Other generation schemes were made through random selection in a deterministic fashion, followed by tuning to create a realistic result. Creatures were often generated by mixing and matching random parts from a library, and then adjusting the underlying skeleton so that the creature appeared realistic; a creature with a tiny body could not support a giant head, for example. To create behaviour for the creatures generated by the procedural generation system, the system tags objects that it creates, and then assigns creatures various affinity levels 

No Man's Sky is a 2016 video game developed by the British development studio, Hello Games. No Man's Sky allows the player to partake in four principal activities—exploration, survival, combat, and trading—in a shared, deterministic, procedurally generated open universe, which contains over 18 quintillion (1.8×1019) planets each with their own unique environment and flora and fauna. The concept of No Man's Sky is based on a long-time desire by Hello Games' founder, Sean Murray, to create a space exploration game that captured the vision and optimism of science fiction writings and art of the 1970s and 1980s. Seeing the game as a landmark title for the studio, Murray led Hello Games towards financial stability with their Joe Danger titles and then began working on the game with a small team of four. The game was formally revealed during the 2013 VGX Awards, following which Murray brought on more staff to complete the title over the next three years.

A seed (star position → planet position → local seed) gets fed through the same generation rules — L-systems for plants, skeleton/part-assembly for creatures, noise functions for terrain. The generation system creates all features of the universe exactly the same way every time this process runs with the same seed, using the repeatability of pseudorandom number generators. That computation happens locally, on your machine, when you arrive somewhere — there's no need for an external observer system because the "decision" of what a planet looks like is just math on a seed.

**Nothing evolves on its own between visits.** Procedural generation starts from scratch for any new visitor to a planet, with the same initial factors being fed into the algorithm — so each player sees the same species and behaviors, if not identical individuals, and species extinctions don't appear to be possible. There's no persistent simulation running in the background that ages or mutates a creature population while you're not looking.

**What does look like "evolution" is dev-authored, not emergent.** Hello Games periodically alters the generation algorithms themselves — during the Origins update, changes to procedural generation refreshed the entire universe, including previously visited planets, turning pristine beaches into volcanic hellscapes. That's a patch changing the rulebook, then the same deterministic engine re-running with the new rules — not a separate system "choosing" when to intervene.

So the honest answer: an outside meta-system observing and steering ecosystem evolution independent of the shipped code isn't something data miners have found, and it wouldn't fit the architecture — the seed-to-output pipeline is the whole mechanism. What you're describing would basically require Hello Games to be running a hidden live service against player telemetry, which isn't part of any documented build.

The user is pointing out that if No Man's Sky uses a deterministic algorithm, Hello Games should be able to explain their exact decision-making process—but they claim they can't. This gets at something real about procedural generation systems: even when they're fully algorithmic, the sheer complexity of layered noise functions, L-systems, and combinatorial parameter spaces can make the outputs genuinely difficult for developers to predict or articulate after the fact. It's like asking for the 10 millionth digit of pi - it's fully deterministic and explainable in principle, but you can't know it without computing it. I should also consider whether Hello Games has actually struggled to explain planetary changes, or if the user is conflating two different things: when updates change generation rules, the same seed produces different output through the updated algorithm (which is explainable), versus being unable to predict what a specific seed will generate without running it (which is just computational irreducibility - sometimes the only way to know an outcome is to actually execute the rules, even though they're fully determined).Good pushback — let me separate two different things that are getting merged: "deterministic" and "explainable/predictable in advance" are not the same thing.

**What "baked in" actually means here:** the rules — the L-system grammar for plants, the skeleton/part library for creatures, the noise functions for terrain — are fully written by Hello Games. They can absolutely tell you *what the rules are*. What they generally can't do (and have said as much) is tell you, off the top of their head, what a specific seed will produce without actually running it. That's not because a hidden system decided something outside the code — it's because complex generative systems are what's sometimes called computationally irreducible: the only way to know the output of the rule is to execute it, even when every step of the rule is fully known and was written by a person.

A concrete parallel: nobody, including the person who wrote the formula, can tell you the 10-millionth digit of pi "and why it makes that decision" without computing it. That doesn't mean there's a second, separate system choosing digits of pi behind the scenes. It means a fully deterministic process can still be unpredictable-in-advance and hard to narrate after the fact, just because of how many steps and combinations are involved.

**On "how does the engine choose to update a planet":** two different mechanisms get called "updates," and conflating them makes it feel mysterious:

- **Same seed, same rules, revisit** → same result every time. Nothing "updates." This is why two players see the same creatures on the same planet.
- **Same seed, changed rules (a Hello Games patch)** → different result. This is the Origins-style refresh where beaches became volcanic hellscapes. The "decision" to change wasn't the engine choosing anything — it was developers changing the ruleset, then the same old deterministic pipeline re-running against it.

There's no third category where the game is quietly evolving ecosystems live based on observation, independent of a patch. If there were, data miners — who've pulled apart the generation code in detail — would have found the hooks for it (network calls it shouldn't need, telemetry-driven parameters, a live-tuning service). Nobody's found that. What they have found is a big, combinatorially rich, but fully local and inspectable rule system.

So the "why can't they explain it" observation is real, but it's evidence of complexity, not of a separate hidden system.

That doesn't mean there's a second, separate system choosing digits of pi behind the scenes. It means a fully deterministic process can still be unpredictable-in-advance and hard to narrate after the fact, just because of how many steps and combinations are involved.

**On "how does the engine choose to update a planet":** two different mechanisms get called "updates," and conflating them makes it feel mysterious:

- **Same seed, same rules, revisit** → same result every time. Nothing "updates." This is why two players see the same creatures on the same planet.
- **Same seed, changed rules (a Hello Games patch)** → different result. This is the Origins-style refresh where beaches became volcanic hellscapes. The "decision" to change wasn't the engine choosing anything — it was developers changing the ruleset, then the same old deterministic pipeline re-running against it.

There's no third category where the game is quietly evolving ecosystems live based on observation, independent of a patch. If there were, data miners — who've pulled apart the generation code in detail — would have found the hooks for it (network calls it shouldn't need, telemetry-driven parameters, a live-tuning service). Nobody's found that. What they have found is a big, combinatorially rich, but fully local and inspectable rule system.

So the "why can't they explain it" observation is real, but it's evidence of complexity, not of a separate hidden system.

Ah, that's the key insight — Hello Games' own patch notes explicitly describe their terrain and creature generation as "evolved," which means they're literally using the same underlying L-system and template libraries that get incrementally refined with each update rather than rebuilt from scratch. That explains the pattern perfectly: it genuinely looks like directional evolutionary progression because that's exactly what's happening in the code.Okay — found it. Straight answer, no hedging:

**The generation code itself has a lineage, and Hello Games literally calls that process "evolving" it.** Their own Worlds Part 2 patch notes state the terrain generation algorithm has been evolved and refined to generate more diverse planetary shapes, with mountains, deep valleys, and sprawling plains — and specific improvements were made to reduce repeating patterns and expand the range of shapes on a single world. Same pattern shows up across creature/plant systems: new species types and biome-specific life get added on top of the existing skeleton/template libraries rather than the whole system being torn out and rebuilt.

That's the mechanism you're watching. Here's why it looks evolutionary and isn't random:

**It's not a from-scratch reroll each patch — it's the same codebase being extended.** The core generation system — the skeleton templates, the L-system grammars for plants, the "blueprint → accessories → layering → scaling" pipeline for creatures — stays intact across updates. Each major update doesn't replace that system, it adds new branches onto it: new part libraries, new biome tags, new species slotted into the existing rule structure. So when Worlds Part 2 shipped, it added new tentacled mollusc species and new bioluminescent creatures specifically tuned for the new purple star systems and deep-ocean environments, layered onto the pre-existing generation rules rather than generated by some new independent process.

**That produces a directional, lineage-like pattern because it genuinely is one** — just a software lineage, not a biological one. Each update's creature/plant additions are built by the same team, using the same underlying templates, informed by what the last update did. That's why you can watch it and see something that looks like progression rather than noise: it's cumulative software development on a shared codebase, which is a real "evolutionary path" in the engineering sense — direction, inheritance, incremental refinement — even though no biological evolution algorithm is running.

**What's NOT happening:** there's no live system watching your planet and deciding to upgrade its specific fauna while you're not looking. The "no listed mechanism for a planet to upgrade" observation is correct — because the upgrade doesn't happen to a planet, it happens to the shared rule library, and then reapplies universe-wide (or to new star classes) the next time you load in. Terrain in existing systems has not been regenerated in some of these updates specifically to avoid resetting player bases — meaning Hello Games is explicit about when a change touches what you've already got versus only new content going forward.

So: the "evolution" is real, it's just one level up from where you were looking for it — in the studio's own generation codebase across patches, not in a hidden per-planet observer.

The subject of this article is from the Worlds Part I update. The information from this article is up-to-date as of 3 September, 2024. Procedural Generation is a mathematical design tool. ... No Man's Sky is a game built on procedural generation; that is, each planet, creature, ship, multi-tool and other items are created procedurally using algorithms in the game itself, rendering diversity through each item created. The following is taken from Wikipedia[1]. The term procedural refers to the process that computes a particular function. Fractals are geometric patterns which can often be generated procedurally. Commonplace procedural content includes textures and meshes. Sound is often also procedurally generated, and has applications in both speech synthesis as well as music. It has been used to create compositions in various genres of electronic music by artists such as Brian Eno who popularized the term "generative music".

Almost all objects in the No Man's Sky universe are procedurally generated. The few that are not procedurally generated are the names of the first five galaxies, expedition rewards and more. These are some, but not by a long shot all, of the procedurally generated objects in the game: ... The player's starting starship as of Beyond, Radiant Pillar BC1, is actually procedurally generated. It is always the same due to it being generated immediately on the start of a world, and the IGS (In-Game Seed) is always the same. The IGS differs from the LSS (Local System Seed) in that the LSS is essentially the system's RNG algorithm, whereas the IGS is run by the game itself. ↑ Procedural generation. Wikipedia. content.title: The Wonders of Worlds: Creation and Procedural Generation in No Man's Sky
content.text:
These algorithms are altered from time to time to change the possible combinations allowable within the game engine. Back during their Origins update, their adjustments to procedural generation refreshed the entire universe, including previously ...

The characteristics of that creation, whether it is the deep crevices along planetary seafloors, the roaming herds of aliens, or the hues of grasses being flicked around by the wind, are generated using a series of algorithms produced by HelloGames themselves. These algorithms are altered from time to time to change the possible combinations allowable within the game engine. Back during their Origins update, their adjustments to procedural generation refreshed the entire universe, including previously visited and colonized planets, resulting in chaos as pristine sand-swept beaches could be utterly transformed into hostile volcanic hellscapes. Not ideal for a beach house a player might have recently built, but cool nonetheless. This is not to say that HelloGames is not designing creature models, multi-tools, weather effects, the textures of water, the sky's palette, or the visual components of a starship - far from it. But their procedural-generative engine is at the heart of their desi

On a personal level, I found their Companions update quite charming, in so far as it introduced alien pet companions to the game. Now, all these kooky and cute creatures I was stumbling upon planet-hopping, had a purpose behind merely surveying and cataloguing. With this update, you could finally raise and nurture them, as well as ride, genetically-alter, and trade their eggs with others. Another favourite addition to this sandbox was the Aquarius update that brought fishing into planetary waters, with complementary features like a deployable Exo-Skiff, new recipes, and fishing records enhancing the experience as well. But in the past year, two updates, both united in spirit, have made tremendous advancements in the sandbox that require a special shout out: Worlds Part 1 and Worlds Part 2. Both updates have pushed the galactic boundaries of No Man's Sky's original design to new limits.

It's a fair question. Let's review the fundamentals of No Man's Sky's world design. At the heart of the game's galactic vastness, which allegedly contains 18 quintillion planets (though counting would be a fool's errand), is their procedural generation engine. For those out of the loop, procedural generation is "a method of creating data algorithmically as opposed to manually, typically through a combination of human-generated content and algorithms coupled with computer-generated randomness and processing power." Most video games have manually created worlds developed for players to inhabit or play through. This could include the village of Stardew Valley, a crowded player hub in Guild Wars 2, or a multiplayer map for Battlefield 1. In fact, this is often so apparent that it is considered the default understanding of video game development for many people.

But procedural generation uses data and algorithms, which have become synonymous with evil machinations of Big Tech, to produce radically unique alternatives for video game worlds and the players that explore them. While procedural generation is not exclusive to No Man's Sky (the practice has existed for as long as video games have been developed), Hello Games undeniably leveled-up what this could mean for video game development, purely due to the sheer scale of their design feat. This is how it works. Everything within No Man's Sky's universe is oriented around the creation and modification of a single initial seed - which is an arbitrary code for a procedural-generated digital world. Minecraft or Valheim can create nearly infinite variations of seeds, because they can be played offline as well, but a single seed is needed in No Man's Sky to create a single universe shared by players across different platforms, times, and places.

All life is spawned initially by a process called procedural generation - in this case a rules engine using a bio-mathematical field called L-systems - underlying the production of the natural features in the game. Whilst it uses mathematical noise and chaos theory, it is not simply random, as TheSeaOfThySoul[2] points out: “The rules of the game dictate how the world works... ecosystems are cohesive, and environments are structured as if hand designed, because they make sense within the rules crafted.” · Whilst procedural generation will start from scratch for any new visitor to a planet, the initial factors being fed into the algorithm should be identical, such that each character will see the same types of creatures and behaviours, if not the identical individuals (unless two characters are close enough to each other); indeed it appears that species extinctions are not possible.

No Man's Sky features a procedurally generated open universe of 18 quintillion planets, which means the game is generated algorithmically rather than manually. It is the first game to use procedural generation to the extent it does.[1] Nearly all elements of the game are procedurally generated, including solar systems, planets and their ecosystems, flora, fauna and their behavioral patterns, artificial structures, and alien factions and their spacecraft. The game's engine employs several algorithms that can mimic a wide range of geometry and structure found in nature. Art elements created by human artists are used and altered as well within these generation systems. The game's audio, including ambient sounds and its underlying soundtrack, also use procedural generation methods from base samples developed by Paul Weir and the musical group 65daysofstatic.

What is the environment like? What kind of creature is it? Where is it in the food chain? What will it prey on, what will prey on it? How will it interact with other creatures? content.title: How No Man's Sky creator is using clever tech to build a truly indie game universe - GamesBeat
content.text:
Sean Murray isn’t creating just one new world. He’s creating a whole universe of them in his sci-fi game No Man’s Sky, which uses a clever technology to mathematically generate new worlds for players to explore. This “procedural” technology has been around for a while, but it hasn’t been used on this scale before. And the remarkable thing about it is that it is so efficient at generating random worlds that Hello Games, Murray’s studio in Guildford, England, in the United Kingdom, doesn’t have to have massive data centers to store all the data associated with the worlds. It may sound geeky, but these algorithms will enable Hello Games to create enormous worlds with a team of just 10 people. That’s important, because Murray doesn’t want to raise a ton of money or create a gigantic team with money from big publishers. He wants to be independent and keep control of his own creation.

Sean Murray: I’ll start by explaining the HUD, which gets to some of the things you do in the game. It has the name of the planet you’re on. It’s procedurally generated. Two people fly down to this same planet, they’ll see the same thing. Everyone’s in the same shared universe. But the universe is really big. You’re not likely to visit the same planet as somebody else. If you’re the first person on that planet, you’ll be the one who discovered it, but you don’t claim it until you go to a beacon. Then you upload that discovery. You can also name it at that point. Then you’d name it – probably something rude – and the next person who touches down sees the name you gave it instead and sees that you discovered it. If you make a discovery, you get money for it, what we call units. Money buys bigger ships, better ships, and better weapons than the weapons on the ground.

Sean Murray of Hello Games at E3 2015. GamesBeat: Even though it’s challenging in a lot of ways, there’s a nice renaissance now for indies. Murray: Absolutely. In the 8-bit days, or 16-bit, a decision was made to go down a certain route, a more cinematic, filmic route for games. The industry really chased after that. Indies have almost gone back 10 or 15 years to explore the alternate realities that could have existed. That’s what I think about Braid. Braid could have happened 15 years ago. So could Limbo and Retro City Rampage and a whole bunch of other games. They’ve gone back in time to the Amiga or something and said, “What if things had gone this direction?” · For us that’s sort of true as well. This kind of game existed more back then, even on the Amstrad or the C64 – games like Freescape and Elite. It was procedurally generated, a huge open universe.

Murray: When you’re standing here, what you see around you is generated around you. If you fly away, it’s thrown away. If you fly back it’s generated again. Everything will always be the same, though. It’s a formula where the input is where you stand and the output is what you see. Since the input is the same, the output is the same. Based on what we’ve shown so far, the think people have picked up that’s most different about the game is the exploration. That’s one way to play the game. If I find something rare, quite difficult to find, when I upload it at the beacon it’ll be worth more. ... Murray: Kind of like random loot drops. They’ll give me money sometimes or technology.

content.title: No Man’s Sky: A Vast Game Crafted by Algorithms | MIT Technology Review
content.text:
Sean Murray, one of the creators of the computer game No Man’s Sky, can’t guarantee that the virtual universe he is building is infinite, but he’s certain that, if it isn’t, nobody will ever find out. “If you were to visit one virtual planet every second,” he says, “then our own sun will have died before you’d have seen them all.” · No Man’s Sky is a video game quite unlike any other. Developed for Sony’s PlayStation 4 by an improbably small team (the original four-person crew has grown only to 10 in recent months) at Hello Games, an independent studio in the south of England, it’s a game that presents a traversable universe in which every rock, flower, tree, creature, and planet has been “procedurally generated” to create a vast and diverse play area. “We are attempting to do things that haven’t been done before,” says Murray.

Sean Murray, one of the creators of the computer game No Man’s Sky, can’t guarantee that the virtual universe he is building is infinite, but he’s certain that, if it isn’t, nobody will ever find out. “If you were to visit one virtual planet every second,” he says, “then our own sun will have died…

Sean Murray, one of the creators of the computer game No Man’s Sky, can’t guarantee that the virtual universe he is building is infinite, but he’s certain that, if it isn’t, nobody will ever find out. “If you were to visit one virtual planet every second,” he says, “then our own sun will have died before you’d have seen them all.” · No Man’s Sky is a video game quite unlike any other. Developed for Sony’s PlayStation 4 by an improbably small team (the original four-person crew has grown only to 10 in recent months) at Hello Games, an independent studio in the south of England, it’s a game that presents a traversable universe in which every rock, flower, tree, creature, and planet has been “procedurally generated” to create a vast and diverse play area. “We are attempting to do things that haven’t been done before,” says Murray.

“Players will even be able to mark the planet as toxic or radioactive, or indicate what kind of life is there and then that then appears on everyone’s map,” says Murray. Experimentation has been a watchword throughout the game’s production. Originally the game was entirely randomly generated. “Only around 1 percent of the time would it create something that looked natural, interesting, and pleasing to the eye; the rest of the time it was a mess and, in some cases where the sky, the water, and the terrain were all the same color, unplayable,” Murray says. So the team began to create simple rules, such as the distance from a sun at which it is likely that there will be moisture,” he explains. “From that we decide there will be rivers, lakes, erosion, and weather, all of which is dependent on what the liquid is made from. The color of the water in the atmosphere will derive from what the liquid is; we model the refractions to give you a modeled atmosphere.” ·

This presents numerous technological challenges, not least of which is how to test a universe of such scale during its development – the team is currently using virtual testers—automated bots that wander around taking screenshots which are then sent back to the team for viewing. Additionally, while No Man’s Sky might have an infinite-sized universe, there aren’t an infinite number of players. To avoid the problem of a kind of virtual loneliness, where a player might never encounter another person on his or her travels, the game starts every new player in the same galaxy (albeit on his or her own planet) with a shared initial goal of traveling to its center. Later in the game, players can meet up, fight, trade, mine, and explore. “Ultimately we don’t know whether people will work, congregate, or disperse,” Murray says. “I know players don’t like to be told that we don’t know what will happen, but that’s what is exciting to us: the game is a vast experiment.” ·

That's the core tradeoff, and it's not sentimentality or control-freakery, it's math:

A game world has no equivalent unless someone defines one — and defining "what makes a good planet" turns out to require exactly the kind of judgment calls (does this creature's proportions look plausible, is this terrain traversable, does this color palette feel alien vs. nauseating) that right now only a human eye reliably makes. A live evolutionary process would mean the planet you found in 2016 keeps drifting even when nobody's watching — which breaks the "the math never changes" guarantee that lets thousands of people share one universe without a server tracking every planet's live state.

Here's the real answer, and it's not "they didn't think of it" — it's that **the fitness function is the entire problem, and it's exactly as expensive as the patches you're trying to replace.**

**A fitness function needs a judge, and "is this planet/creature good" doesn't have a computable one.** In natural evolution, the fitness function is external and free — the environment kills what doesn't work, no design cost. In a game, someone has to write the evaluator that decides which mutations survive. "Does this creature look plausible," "is this terrain traversable," "does this ecosystem feel coherent" — those are exactly the judgment calls Murray's team found required a human eye when the original fully-random version produced unplayable results 99% of the time. Swapping "random" for "evolutionary with a fitness function" doesn't remove that need, it just relocates it: now instead of hand-tuning the rules directly, you're hand-tuning the scoring function that decides what survives — which is the same design labor wearing a different hat.

**Bad fitness functions get exploited, not satisfied.** This is well documented in actual genetic-algorithm research: evolutionary systems ruthlessly find whatever technically scores well, even when that's degenerate — the classic examples are evolved virtual creatures that learn to vibrate or glitch through the floor to "win" a locomotion fitness test instead of actually walking. An unsupervised evolutionary content system would do the same to any aesthetic/diversity metric you gave it, and catching and patching those exploits is itself a content update — so the "no more updates" premise breaks from the inside.

**There's precedent for exactly this attempt, and it needed constant human curation anyway.** Spore tried a version of this — player-and-algorithm-driven creature evolution with shared traits propagating through a population. Even there, "evolution" was really constrained procedural assembly plus heavy player/editorial steering, not an autonomous unsupervised process left to run — because letting it run truly unsupervised produced the same degenerate/incoherent results problem.

Right now NMS avoids that entirely: it's stateless math, computed fresh from a seed, discarded when you leave. Murray built the studio's whole model — a ~10-person team, no data centers — around that statelessness. A genuinely evolutionary content engine reintroduces the infrastructure cost he specifically designed around.

But that's narrative framing bolted onto the deterministic-seed engine underneath; it's not literally what's computing the planets. The lore explains the universe in-fiction as if a mind curates it. The code just runs math on a seed. So the parallel is clever but it's fiction wrapping code, not evidence the code works that way.

**On the literal engineering proposal — could an AI actually serve as the judge/fitness function?** Yes, this is a real, existing technique (learned reward models / neural critics used in procedural content generation research), and it would solve part of what I described as the blocker. But it doesn't dissolve the problem, it relocates it again, in three specific ways:

1. **The judge still needs to be trained on "good," and that training data is human-curated.** Somebody has to label or score thousands of example creatures/terrains as good/bad/coherent to train the judge in the first place. 2. **A trained judge gets gamed.** This is the reward-hacking / Goodhart's law problem from RL research: an evolutionary generator optimizing against a learned judge will find whatever exploits the judge's blind spots — degenerate shapes that score high but look wrong, the same way evolved virtual creatures learn to glitch through floors instead of walking. You'd need ongoing monitoring to catch and patch judge failures, which is, again, an update.

3. **The judge doesn't invent new categories.** A judge trained to recognize "good creature" or "good terrain" can filter within those categories — it can't invent gas giants, fishing, or pet breeding. Those are new mechanics a designer decided to add. No fitness function derives "let players ride the plants" from "score this plant's plausibility." So even a great AI judge only removes the *curation* half of updates, not the *new content type* half.

Where I'd land: an AI judge is the single most promising real path toward what you're describing, and it's plausible Hello Games could ship a small trained model client-side to keep determinism intact. It would probably shrink the update cycle a lot. It wouldn't eliminate it, because the two remaining costs — training data curation and reward-hacking defense — are the same kind of ongoing human judgment call as before, just applied less often and at a different point in the pipeline.

The key insight is that such a model wouldn't discover objective truth about what's "good," but rather learn the distribution of Hello Games' design choices and aesthetic direction—the patterns in how they've chosen to improve and evolve the game. A model trained this way could plausibly judge whether newly generated creatures or terrain feel consistent with the established style and complexity progression, or extrapolate incremental continuations that follow the historical trajectory. But it's still fundamentally bounded by what's in the training data—it can interpolate and recombine patterns, but it can't generate genuinely novel directions that fall outside the existing design space.

I'm thinking through the Atlas expedition concept the user proposed—it's creative game design brainstorming, so I should engage with genuine critical thinking rather than just agreeing with everything. I want to give honest feedback on what works and what the real risks might be, matching their collaborative tone while staying true to being genuinely helpful.

Expeditions are an actual proven mechanic in No Man's Sky with real community engagement, and the narrative arc idea has precedent in how the game has handled lore before. A six-month revelation could genuinely build momentum. But here's the tension: six months is dramatically longer than any existing expedition, and more importantly, Hello Games has specific historical scar tissue from 2016 when they overpromised at launch and faced a PR disaster. That's a concrete, relevant risk worth raising honestly—the technical work around reward hacking and new mechanics still isn't solved by marketing framing alone, and NMS players and the studio itself are probably sensitive to big public commitments before the technical foundation is solid.Marketing logic checks out — NMS's playerbase has already shown it responds hard to "something big is happening" framing (Origins, the anniversary updates, the Worlds Part 1/2 rollout each spiked concurrent players noticeably), and expeditions are a proven mechanic for exactly this: time-boxed, narrative-wrapped community events with real rewards at the end. "Birth of Atlas" as a framing device is genuinely good instinct — it takes something abstract (we changed the underlying generation judge) and turns it into a story players can watch unfold, which is basically what good live-service marketing is.

Two things worth being straight about before this becomes a plan rather than a pitch:

**A 6-month expedition would be unprecedented for them, and that's a real risk, not just a scale-up.** Every NMS expedition to date has run a few weeks to at most a couple months. Six months is long enough that it stops being "an event" and starts being "the current state of the game" — which changes what it needs to be. A short expedition can ship a little rough because it's temporary and forgiven fast. Something billed as six months long gets judged the way a permanent feature does, by people who've been in it since week one and are tired of it by week ten.

**Hello Games specifically has scar tissue about this exact failure mode.** The 2016 launch disaster wasn't that the tech was bad — it's that they let hype outrun what was actually finished and shipped, and got hammered for years afterward. Announcing "Atlas is being born" as a headline event puts a specific, watched spotlight exactly on the part of this whole conversation that isn't solved yet — reward-hacking defense on a live judge, and the fact that a judge alone doesn't invent new mechanics. If the community expedition is billed as "watch the universe evolve" and what they actually see for stretches of it is the judge producing degenerate shapes while the team patches the reward function, that's the highest-visibility possible way to expose the unfinished part.

The version of this that avoids that trap: build and stress-test Atlas quietly first — the boring reward-hacking-defense work — then launch "Birth of Atlas" as the reveal of something already load-bearing, not as the six-month live debugging session. Same marketing payoff, without turning the hardest unsolved engineering problem in this whole thread into the thing a million people are watching in real time.

I should focus on providing practical guidance for sourcing quality Corvette parts, considering factors like OEM versus aftermarket options, reputable suppliers, and what to look for when evaluating parts.Corvettes were added in the Voyagers update and got expanded again in Remnant (6.2), so if you haven't touched them since launch there's more to work with now. On actually getting parts worth using:

**Where good parts come from (in order of yield):**
- Buy simple ones straight from any Space Station's Corvette Workshop, and trade at the Workshop's module counter — decent baseline stuff, not the best.
- **Derelict Freighters** are the best source — the end terminal reward gives 3–5 random corvette modules per run, and this is where the stat-heavy stuff tends to show up.
- Salvageable scrap on planets, crashed freighters on planet surfaces, and Frigate Expedition mission rewards all drop modules too.
- Hunting pirates and shooting cargo pods off freighters is a slower but steady source if you want to farm specifically.

**On what actually makes a part "worth a fuck":** most parts give a stat/slot boost, but only for the first 3 of that type you place — the boost differs depending on whether it's the 1st, 2nd, or 3rd of that type, so the trick is placing your best-rolled part in whichever slot order gives it the biggest bonus, not just slapping down whatever you find first. Beyond 3 of a type, extra copies are cosmetic only.

**Cockpit specifics** — you only get one, so it's worth being picky: Titan gives the highest boost percentage, Ambassador is better for maneuverability, and Thunderbird is the streamlined/practical option. Titan and Ambassador both run 1,600,000 units from the Workshop if you just want to buy one outright rather than farm it.

**Best-in-slot main engine currently:** the Arcadia Heavy Booster — highest maneuverability and booster strength of any main engine — but it's not purchasable, only obtainable through salvage or trading, so that one specifically means derelict freighters or player trading, not the Workshop counter.

**Practical note on class:** don't over-prioritize S-class chasing — a well-built C-class with the Arcadia Heavy Booster will outperform a poorly-built S-class, so farm for the right parts before you sink nanites into class upgrades (upgrading to S-class runs roughly 85,000 nanites across multiple steps).

summaries.summary: Synthesized sourcing strategies for quality Corvette components.

content.text:
Corvettes were added in the Voyagers update and got expanded again in Remnant (6.2), so if you haven't touched them since launch there's more to work with now. On actually getting parts worth using:

**Where good parts come from (in order of yield):**
- Buy simple ones straight from any Space Station's Corvette Workshop, and trade at the Workshop's module counter — decent baseline stuff, not the best.
- **Derelict Freighters** are the best source — the end terminal reward gives 3–5 random corvette modules per run, and this is where the stat-heavy stuff tends to show up.
- Salvageable scrap on planets, crashed freighters on planet surfaces, and Frigate Expedition mission rewards all drop modules too.
- Hunting pirates and shooting cargo pods off freighters is a slower but steady source if you want to farm specifically.

**On what actually makes a part "worth a fuck":** most parts give a stat/slot boost, but only for the first 3 of that type you place — the boost differs depending on whether it's the 1st, 2nd, or 3rd of that type, so the trick is placing your best-rolled part in whichever slot order gives it the biggest bonus, not just slapping down whatever you find first. Beyond 3 of a type, extra copies are cosmetic only.

**Cockpit specifics** — you only get one, so it's worth being picky: Titan gives the highest boost percentage, Ambassador is better for maneuverability, and Thunderbird is the streamlined/practical option. Titan and Ambassador both run 1,600,000 units from the Workshop if you just want to buy one outright rather than farm it.

**Best-in-slot main engine currently:** the Arcadia Heavy Booster — highest maneuverability and booster strength of any main engine — but it's not purchasable, only obtainable through salvage or trading, so that one specifically means derelict freighters or player trading, not the Workshop counter.

**Practical note on class:** don't over-prioritize S-class chasing — a well-built C-class with the Arcadia Heavy Booster will outperform a poorly-built S-class, so farm for the right parts before you sink nanites into class upgrades (upgrading to S-class runs roughly 85,000 nanites across multiple steps).

If you want, I can pull the full part list with stat breakdowns by tier so you're not guessing which drops are actually good versus just cosmetic.

content.text:
They differ in aesthetics and stat weighting. Titan gives the highest Boost percentage. Ambassador is better for Maneuverability. Both are 1,600,000 Units from the Workshop, so pick whichever design you prefer and upgrade later.

When you’re done, finalize the build. The Corvette gets added to your starship collection and takes up one starship slot. You can edit it again any time at any Corvette Workshop. Cockpit. There are three design styles: Titan, Ambassador, and Thunderbird. They differ in aesthetics and stat weighting. Titan gives the highest Boost percentage. Ambassador is better for Maneuverability. Both are 1,600,000 Units from the Workshop, so pick whichever design you prefer and upgrade later. Main Engine. The best all-around engine is the Arcadia Heavy Booster. It gives the highest Maneuverability and Booster strength. It’s not available to buy, so look for it through salvage or trading. Reactor. Each reactor type trades off differently: Pick based on how you play. If you warp frequently, Zenith. If you spend a lot of time in combat or tight spaces, Ceto or Medusa.

S-class gives the highest stat ceiling, but the modules themselves matter as much as the class rating. A well-built C-class with the Arcadia Heavy Booster will outperform a poorly-built S-class in most situations. Once you have one, the Corvette replaces the Exocraft for most planetary exploration. You fly low over a planet and scan from the cockpit without landing. Jump out directly onto the planet surface from the side hatch. Several Reddit players have noted that exocrafts feel obsolete once you have a working Corvette set up, though the Pilgrim and Nomad still have advantages for dense, close-range terrain work. The interior base-building aspect is what makes it genuinely different from any other ship. You can install a Refiner Unit inside, set up storage, and build it out as a mobile base. As of update 6.2 (Remnant, February 2026), other players in multiplayer can help decorate your Corvette interior, and you can redecorate while the ship is in flight.

Corvettes were added in the Voyagers update (version 6.0, August 2025). They’re fully modular spaceships you assemble part by part at the Corvette Workshop in any Space Station. You can walk around inside them, decorate the interior, install a refiner, and scan planets from the cockpit without landing. A lot of players use them as a flying base. Browse all available corvette parts on the site. Here’s how to build one and what to prioritize. Every Space Station has a Corvette Workshop. When you land, head toward the shops and look for the four blue teleport columns on the left side. Step through one to reach the Workshop terminal. ... There’s also a Workshop Cache with over 100 storage slots dedicated to Corvette modules. Anything in the cache appears as available when building or trading, so move parts there to keep your exosuit inventory clear.

Go to any Space Station and take the blue teleport columns on the left side of the shop area to reach the Corvette Workshop console. Buy the basic modules you need, then select Create New Corvette to start building. Buying all required basic modules from the Workshop costs around 7,630,000 Units. You can reduce this significantly by salvaging parts from scrap on planets, derelict freighters, and pirate drops. At minimum: 2 Landing Gear, 2 Thrusters, 1 Cockpit, 1 Landing Bay (Access Module), 1 Habitation Module, 1 Reactor, 1 Main Engine, and 1 Weapon System. Set your Corvette as your primary ship, then visit the Starship Outfitting Terminal at any Space Station.

content.text:
Fair — let me correct that, because I oversold it. Straight from the wiki: the Ambassador cockpit functions similarly to a C-class Pulse Engine upgrade — moderate performance boost, maneuverability and boost. C-class. Not S-class, not anything special. Titan's is in the same tier, just weighted toward boost % instead of maneuverability.

So you're right to call that shitty. The community consensus in the discussion threads backs you up hard on this:

- One player straight up said: **the parts aren't what makes your ship powerful, mostly cosmetic — it's the upgrades that always work the best.** Corvette cockpit stats cap out modest regardless of which style you pick.
- Another: the difference between cockpit styles is so marginal after slotting in S & X tech mods that it barely registers.
- There's active confusion in the community about whether cockpit "class" even moves past C at all — multiple players report the pilot cabin staying locked at C no matter what they install, with the actual power coming from upgrading the whole corvette's class through the Starship Outfitting Terminal with nanites, same system as a regular ship, completely separate from which cockpit skin you picked.

**What that means practically:** don't hunt for a "good" cockpit like it's a rare-tier item — Titan/Ambassador/Thunderbird are a design-style choice with a small built-in bonus attached, not a power slot worth grinding derelict freighters for. The actual power comes from:
1. Upgrading the corvette itself to S-class via nanites at the Outfitting Terminal (~85,000 nanites total)
2. Then buying/installing S-class tech upgrades into the tech slots the same way you would on any starship — those numbers dwarf whatever the cockpit itself grants
3. Farming parts like the Arcadia Heavy Booster (main engine) matter more, since that one's genuinely best-in-slot and not purchasable, only found via salvage/trade

So pick whichever cockpit looks the way you want your ship to look, upgrade the ship class with nanites, then dump good tech mods in the slots — that's where "worth a fuck" actually comes from, not the cockpit part itself.

content.title: Corvette Parts (All) | No Man's Sky Resources
content.text:
Once a Corvette's structure is finalized, you can add internal decorations by stepping inside the ship and accessing the Build Menu. This has no part limit. The structure of a finalized Corvette can be also modified at the Corvette Workshop at any time. Corvettes are a completely bespoke class of starship - assembled piece by piece - with a traversable, furnished interior. These habitable ships are constructed in a similar fashion to planetary bases, and can be fitted out internally with living areas such as nutrition units and bunk beds. ... Buy simple ones from Space Station. Trade with the Space Station Corvette Module. Dig up Salvagable Scrap on planets. Crashed Freighters on Planets. Missions from Nexus, Space Station, Corvette, etc. Frigate Expedition Missions. Hunting Pirates. Shooting Cargo Pods on Freighters. Derelict Freighter end terminal rewards 3-5 random corvette modules.

Begin Corvette creation at a Corvette Workshop, found aboard Space Stations by the large landing pads near the station entrance tunnel. A number of basic modules can also be purchased from the Workshop. Without mods, you can place up to 100 parts. Bear in mind that building too high will begin to obstruct your view when flying this ship. I recommend no higher than 3 floors. Select finalize to complete a Corvette design, or exit the Workshop to resume it later. Most Corvette parts provide some sort of stat or slot boost, for the first 3 parts of a particular type placed. I've noticed though that the numbers change depending on if you're placing part 1, 2 or 3. If you're smart about it, you can get the best boost for each part by placing them in the correct order, for example using one of each of the 3 shield modules, but placing them in the order that gives the best boost for each.

The modules are free, all types can be found, but it's random. ... Optionally, obtain shields, windows, platings, hull attachments, flight stabilisers. Note: The modules have different names which imply different design styles. The functionality of the modules will be the same. Over time, as you collect more, you can swap them out and try different ones, and decide which style you like. Thunderbird - pragmatic and gritty with exposed pipework · Ambassador - elegant, round, soft, clean, retro-futuristic · Titan - militaristic, with many monitoring panels, buttons, gauges, screens ·

Misc: Thunderbird-class corvette parts seem to be directly inspired by the Frontier ship from Starfield with the interior strongly resembling such of a Millenium Falcon from Star-Wars, while the Ambassdor and Titan class interiors seem to be directly inspired by various interiors from the Alien franchise, like the USCSS Nostromo. Some interior designs have typography similar to Semiotic Standard, with repeating signs that mean "WARNING/HAZARD", "RADIATION HAZARD" and an unknown sign that does not seem to exist in the symbol list. Some signs even appear to have different color, though the image itself is not changed.[1] To build a corvette, return to the Corvette Workshop console in the space station and click Create New Corvette. The console will switch you to a build mode. Press Z to get the build menu. Select and place the landing gear first. On top of it place larger modules, such as the habitation.

Attach the cockpit module to the habitation front. Add main engines and reactor where ever it looks good. The ship will fly equally well whether it's symmetrical or asymmetrical. As of Update 6.03 there is a 160 part maximum. Apply your changes. You can also store and continue later. Other players only see applied changes. A name for the ship will automatically be generated, which you can change later. After the outer shape is finished and saved, enter the parked corvette and press Z inside. This opens an interior build menu. Continue to add a bed, refinery, cargo containers, or windows, these are corvette specific modules. Players can also add most buildable items that they'd use on a planetary base. These parts require materials, just as when you build a base. There is no part maximum for inside. (Other than the save-wide 16.000 placeable objects limit ) Just as with a base, you can change the colour of some Corvette parts.

Note: The interior parts can look different in style, too, depending on whether you place them in a Thunderbird, Ambassador, or Titan habitation module. The simplest ship is just one habitation with cockpit, thruster, and access ramp. But the more modules you find, the bigger you can build! Habitation modules have an impact on cargo size and outer Corvette size. You can build several habitations, one after the other (horizontal), or one next to each other (horizontal), or on top of each other (vertical) to build larger corvettes. for horizontally aligned habitations, the game will insert passages for players to walk through. for vertically aligned habitations, enter the bottom floor and open the build menu, and select a ladder module, and place it to go upstairs. Engines have an impact on your speed, you can have several, even a mix of types. You can have a mix of landing gears.

content.title: No Man’s Sky How To Get Corvette Parts
content.text:
All starter parts are C class and cannot be traded up. Select Create new Corvette at the terminal. Place Landing Gear first, then add modules like the Habitation Module, Cockpit, Reactor, Thrusters, Access Module, and Weapon Systems.

The Voyagers update added Corvettes to No Man’s Sky, giving players the chance to build massive modular ships they can walk around in. To get started, you need Corvette parts, which are bought, salvaged, or traded. This guide explains where to get the parts, how to build your ship, and how to upgrade it later. Go to any Space Station. Turn toward the shops, then head left to the four teleporters. Enter one, and you will find the Corvette Workshop. At the terminal, you can buy modules. Grab one of every part, plus two Landing Gears and two Wings to save yourself trouble later. The most expensive parts cost over 1.8 million Units, so make sure you have the funds. All starter parts are C class and cannot be traded up. Select Create new Corvette at the terminal. Place Landing Gear first, then add modules like the Habitation Module, Cockpit, Reactor, Thrusters, Access Module, and Weapon Systems.

Planets with Salvagable Scrap show a yellow shield symbol. Use your scanner, then excavate with the Terrain Manipulator. Destroy the container to collect modules. These can be equipped or traded at the terminal under Trade Advanced Modules. You can barter up to three modules at once, with better ones improving trade chances. Other reliable sources include missions, derelict freighters, and crashed freighters. Almost every type of space activity has a chance to reward Corvette modules. Corvette parts in No Man’s Sky are easy to buy but harder to upgrade. Basic modules come from the Workshop, while advanced modules must be salvaged, traded, or earned from missions. Build your Corvette with the essentials, then expand it with salvaged upgrades to create a ship that fits your playstyle. Buy starter modules at the Corvette Workshop in any Space Station.

Looking at actual player data, S-class corvettes perform well in raw stats, though DPS comparisons are mixed depending on the loadout—some builds favor dedicated fighter interceptors while others show corvettes holding their own. The community consensus seems to lean toward Sentinel Interceptors as the superior pure fighter class, largely because their slot configuration allows for stacked supercharged upgrades that multiply damage output significantly.

As for the black ship mystery, I'm not entirely certain what mechanic caused that—it could be a freighter fleet expedition variant, an exotic ship reveal, or possibly a documented bug where interceptor hulls change appearance after being removed from inventory. Rather than speculate further, I should acknowledge the uncertainty here and offer to dig deeper if you want specifics on that particular mechanic.**Direct answer: for a pure fighter, no — a well-built Sentinel Interceptor is still going to beat the Corvette, and the community consensus backs that up specifically.** One player who runs high-end builds on both put it plainly: an optimized sentinel interceptor will still be a better pure fighter, even sitting right next to their praise for the corvette overall. That's not "every ship loses to interceptors" bias — it's slot geometry. Interceptors are built with adjacent supercharged slots as their whole design gimmick, and that adjacency bonus is what produces the absurd DPS numbers (one comparison showed 26,000 DPS on an interceptor loadout vs 9,500 on a hauler with the same upgrades, same weapon). Corvettes don't get that slot layout — they're built more like a modular hab/base with combat bolted on, not a purpose-built weapons platform.

**Where the corvette actually wins, and it's not close:** it's not a fighter replacement, it's a different tool —
- Mobile base you can walk around in, portable storage, refiner installed inside
- Autopilot-plus-manual-scanning from the cockpit while hovering, which makes salvage/resource-hotspot farming absurdly efficient — set throttle low, autopilot holds course, you scan out the windshield
- One tester went so far as to say a fully-kitted S-class corvette beat their best S-class starship in every stat except needing a landing pad — but that's stats, not necessarily translating to "better than a dedicated interceptor gunfight."

**And here's the part that actually matters for your specific question:** multiple threads independently note that in real combat, huge DPS gaps often don't matter — a hauler doing 9,500 DPS melts pirates almost as fast as an interceptor doing 26,000, because most enemies die well before either weapon's cooldown becomes the bottleneck. So if what you're doing is standard pirate/sentinel skirmishes and not deliberately hunting the hardest possible fights, the raw fighter-supremacy gap may not be something you feel in practice — you'd be trading a small combat-ceiling loss for a genuinely different, useful capability set (walkable interior, mobile base, scanning workflow).

**Verdict:** don't switch off the interceptor as your fighter. Keep both — interceptor for anything where you specifically want max kill speed, corvette for exploration/farming/base-on-the-move. That's exactly the split the community's landed on, not "corvette replaces everything" or "corvette is weaker so skip it."

So the interceptor can fire much longer, than the hauler, but since the enemies are dead long before even the hauler's cannon overheats, this doesn't matter in practice.

That's a real, standing want in the community, and you're right that it's currently blocked — deliberately, not just an oversight. The Orbital update did add the Starship Fabricator, letting you salvage customization modules from Fighters, Explorers, Haulers, and Solar Ships and build your own from the pieces. But Sentinel Interceptors, Shuttles, Exotics, and Living Ships are explicitly excluded from salvage — you can scrap an interceptor for nanites/materials, but not for build-your-own parts.

Two reasons floating around for why, worth knowing so you're not just waiting on nothing:

Travelers can finally make their own custom ship in No Man's Sky: Orbital.

Of the Expedition Reward ships, only the Iron Vulture can be salvaged for parts. The Starborn Runner and Utopia Speeder do not have distinct parts that can be salvaged. While you can salvage the Iron Vulture, you'll only receive one of its three unique modules. You’ll need at least one of each type of customization module for your desired type to create a custom ship.

As of the Orbital update, No Man’s Sky players can finally create their own custom ships. Travelers have long requested this feature, but after many years, Hello Games has finally released a means of creating new ships from custom parts. ... From how to join a match to the functions of The Nexus, here are some pointers to getting started with co-op in No Man's Sky. ... The process of creating a custom ship is fairly simple. Updated July 29, 2024, by Sean Murray: No Man's Sky continues to evolve, and with it comes new options for custom ship construction.

The first step to creating your custom starship is salvaging customization modules from an existing ship. You can obtain ships for salvaging in one of two ways. You can either purchase the ship from other entities aboard space stations, freighters, or trading posts, or your freighter, or you can find crashed ships on planetary surfaces. This process will destroy the ship you are salvaging. Only salvage parts from a ship you’re okay with losing forever. Once you've obtained a ship, head to the nearest space station and seek out the Starship Outfitting terminal at the back near the station core. The Outfitting terminal is where you previously upgraded ships using nanites or scrapped them for credits. Now you can perform a 'salvage analysis' to determine what customization modules can be extracted.

My mistake. Here's the actual process, confirmed:

**You don't shop for interceptors at stations — you hunt crash sites on dissonant planets.** From the galaxy map, look for a system flagged "Dissonant" instead of a normal biome label. Land, and you're looking for one of several trigger paths:
- Defeat wave 5 of Corrupted Sentinels on a dissonant planet — reveals a Dissonance Spike marking the crash site
- Destroy a Sentinel capital ship (5-star wanted level in space) — awards a Carrier AI Fragment that leads straight to a crash site
- A bespoke space encounter where a garbled-message interceptor warps away and leaves a warp path to follow
- Harmonic Camp terminals, if you've got the override glyphs

**Repair requires farming three specific materials on-site, not credits:**
- **Radiant Shards** — mine the purple crystals with the Advanced Mining Laser, usually plentiful right around the crash site
- **Inverted Mirrors** — from destroying a Dissonance Resonator (the tall insectoid drilling machine), guarded by Corrupted Sentinel drones and quadrupeds, so expect a real fight
- **Harmonic Brain** — salvage a Hyaline Brain from the crashed ship itself, then use "Probe Subconscious" on it, which marks a nearby Ancient Site/Monolith; go there and select "Present Brain" to convert it

Repair the Pilot Interface with those, claim the ship, done.

You're right, I conflated normal-ship station shopping with how interceptors actually work — different system entirely. My mistake. Here's the actual process, confirmed:

**You don't shop for interceptors at stations — you hunt crash sites on dissonant planets.** From the galaxy map, look for a system flagged "Dissonant" instead of a normal biome label. Land, and you're looking for one of several trigger paths:
- Defeat wave 5 of Corrupted Sentinels on a dissonant planet — reveals a Dissonance Spike marking the crash site
- Destroy a Sentinel capital ship (5-star wanted level in space) — awards a Carrier AI Fragment that leads straight to a crash site
- A bespoke space encounter where a garbled-message interceptor warps away and leaves a warp path to follow
- Harmonic Camp terminals, if you've got the override glyphs

**Repair requires farming three specific materials on-site, not credits:**
- **Radiant Shards** — mine the purple crystals with the Advanced Mining Laser, usually plentiful right around the crash site
- **Inverted Mirrors** — from destroying a Dissonance Resonator (the tall insectoid drilling machine), guarded by Corrupted Sentinel drones and quadrupeds, so expect a real fight
- **Harmonic Brain** — salvage a Hyaline Brain from the crashed ship itself, then use "Probe Subconscious" on it, which marks a nearby Ancient Site/Monolith; go there and select "Present Brain" to convert it

Repair the Pilot Interface with those, claim the ship, done.

**One thing worth knowing while you're doing this crawl instead of station-hopping:** the exact aesthetic/style of interceptor is tied to the system it's found in — so repeated dissonance spikes in the same system will always give you the same-looking ship, just potentially different stats/class. So if you want variety in appearance, you need different dissonant systems, not repeat runs in the same one.

And once you do own it — general starship tech upgrades (shields, hyperdrive, etc.) still install normally, it's specifically the core weapon/movement tech that's unique Sentinel-only hardware you can't swap for normal parts.

I replaced the cadmium drive with an S-class module and got some range back but I now have one A-class and 2x S-class modules installed. Three modules only or you get tech overload. So... because the cadmium and emeril drives don't seem to count much (or at all) towards tech limit, leaving them in can give you a modest boost to your hyperdrive range.
